title: Kulich
subtitle: The very rich Russian Easter bread scented with saffron, cardamom, and raisins
excerpt: Kulich is baked for Russian Orthodox Easter and given as a gift. The dough is heavily enriched with eggs, butter, and milk, and flavoured with saffron, cardamom, and raisins. It bakes tall in a cylindrical tin and is glazed with white icing after cooling. The crumb is tender, slightly sweet, and keeps for several days.
sourceNotes: Kulich is the traditional Easter bread of the Russian Orthodox Church, blessed by a priest on Pascha morning and eaten throughout Easter week. The enriched sponge-dough method, saffron, and mixed dried fruit are consistent across Russian and Eastern European culinary literature and have been documented since at least the nineteenth century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze once fully cooled, without the icing. Thaw at room temperature and add the icing glaze just before serving.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Kulich keeps well wrapped for 3 to 4 days. The flavour improves on the second day.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 170 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 155 degrees Celsius. Lower shelf; tent with foil after 20 minutes if the top colours too quickly.

glossaryTerms.definition: A bread-making technique where a portion of the flour, all the liquid, and all the yeast are mixed and left to ferment for 30 to 60 minutes before the remaining flour, butter, eggs, and enrichments are added. The pre-fermented sponge improves flavour, strength, and oven spring in very enriched doughs like kulich and babka.

content.text: Kulich is one of the most enriched breads in European baking. The

gives the yeast a head start before the butter and eggs go in, which is important because fat slows yeast activity. A tall tin is traditional; a clean, greased 15 cm round springform tin lined with a tall collar of baking paper works at home. The oven temperature must be low to stop the top burning before the centre is baked through.

items.prepNote: warm (38 degrees Celsius); steep a pinch of saffron in it for 15 minutes

content.text: Steep the saffron in the warm milk for 15 minutes. Combine 150 g of flour, the yeast, and 20 g of sugar in a large bowl. Pour in the saffron milk and stir to a smooth batter. Cover and leave for 45 to 60 minutes until well risen and bubbly.

items.prepNote: soaked in warm water or rum for 30 minutes, then drained

content.text: Add the remaining flour, sugar, salt, eggs, vanilla, and cardamom to the risen sponge. Mix until a rough dough forms. Knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth.

Add the softened butter in three additions, kneading each addition in fully before adding the next. The dough will look shaggy and greasy at first but will become smooth and elastic. This stage takes 10 to 15 minutes by hand, or 6 to 8 minutes in a stand mixer with the dough hook.

Flatten the dough and scatter the drained raisins and mixed peel across the surface. Fold and press them in, then knead briefly to distribute. Cover and leave at room temperature for 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.

Butter a 15 cm springform tin and line the sides with a collar of baking paper extending 10 cm above the rim. Shape the dough into a round and place it in the tin. Proof for 1 hour until the dough has risen to the level of the tin rim.

Bake at 170 degrees Celsius for 40 to 45 minutes. Cover the top loosely with foil after 20 minutes to prevent over-browning. The kulich is done when an instant-read thermometer reads 93 degrees Celsius at the centre, or when a skewer inserted in the middle comes out clean.
Cool completely in the tin. Unmould, peel away the paper collar, and drizzle with royal icing made from icing sugar and a few drops of water.

A very enriched dough can collapse when turned out if the crumb has not set fully. Cool kulich on its side, rotating it gently every 10 minutes, so the crumb does not sag under its own weight while warm. Once fully cool, it is stable enough to stand upright.
